questions.q: What command finds exactly which Delta table version changed the MERGE's match condition?
options: VACUUM silver.sales_clean
OPTIMIZE silver.sales_clean
SELECT * FROM silver.sales_clean LIMIT 10
DESCRIBE HISTORY silver.sales_clean
questions.explain: DESCRIBE HISTORY is Delta Lake's built-in audit log, showing every write's operation and parameters, including the exact ON clause used.

questions.q: What did version 47's operationParameters show, compared to version 46?
options: Version 47 ran before version 46, so it couldn't be the cause
Version 47 matched on store_id and sale_date; version 46 (and Lesson 5's original) matched on transaction_id
Version 47 was a VACUUM operation, not a MERGE
Both versions used the exact same transaction_id match condition
questions.explain: Version 47, the first MERGE run on or after March 1st, shows the changed ON clause — the exact commit where the pipeline broke.

questions.q: What did the GROUP BY store_id, sale_date HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 query prove?
options: transaction_id has duplicate values across the table
gold.daily_sales_summary and gold.category_breakdown are unrelated tables
Every store_id and sale_date combination in silver.sales_clean is perfectly unique
store_id + sale_date is not a unique key — Store 48 on March 2nd alone had 37 rows sharing that combination
questions.explain: This controlled test returned a real row_count of 37 for one store/day, confirming store_id + sale_date is nowhere close to unique.

questions.q: Mechanically, why does a non-unique match key corrupt the MERGE?
options: Non-unique keys only affect SELECT queries, never MERGE statements
Delta Lake automatically rejects any MERGE with a non-unique key, so no corruption is possible
The MERGE simply runs slower but always produces correct results
One incoming source row can match many target rows, so UPDATE SET * can't apply unambiguously — it errors, overwrites several rows with one row's values, or drops rows during the insert path
questions.explain: Matching one source row against many target rows makes the UPDATE branch ambiguous, which is exactly what produces the data corruption or errors seen downstream.

questions.q: Why is this bug realistic rather than contrived?
options: store_id and sale_date are each individually valid, correctly populated columns — the mistake is treating their combination as a unique key when the business doesn't guarantee that
Because Delta Lake does not support MERGE INTO at all
Because the original transaction_id column was deleted from the schema
Because store_id and sale_date are both invalid columns that should never be queried
questions.explain: The new ON clause reads fine in isolation and would pass a quick review — it only fails once you know a store logs more than one sale per day.
